title: Helix Pharma POC — Practical latency tuning and cost sensitivity report
content:
Executive summary:

This note captures the benchmarking work we ran with Helix Pharma during the week of 2028-07-11. The customer asked for practical knobs they can apply to meet a 95th percentile latency target of <= 220ms for short document QA (avg tokens out ~= 40) at a sustained 40 qps, and for a cost sensitivity analysis that shows tradeoffs between model choice, quantization, and batching.

Key takeaways (short):
- Baseline (fp16, no batching, no prefix cache) with model RDX-3B yields p95 ~ 310ms at 40 qps (single pool, N=8 GPUs). Cost baseline ~ $0.72 per 1k requests.
- Enabling KV prefix caching on repeat prompt patterns reduced p95 to ~190ms for ~35% of traffic where prompt prefix matched cached keys. Global p95 improved to ~250ms.
- Small batching (batch size 4, dynamic window 20ms) improved throughput cost by ~18% with minor p95 regression (~+10ms) when requests are uniform. For bursty arrival patterns batching helps overall cost but can harm tail latency for low-latency tiers.
- 4-bit quantization (int4 via Redwood-compatible build) reduced per-token cost by ~28% with a mild quality delta on long-generation checks; p95 improved ~5–10ms due to faster kernels.
- Recommendation for Helix: combine KV prefix caching + model RDX-3B-int4 + modest batching (max 6, dynamic 15ms) for a projected p95 ~ 210–230ms at 40 qps and cost ~ $0.52 per 1k requests. This meets their target with conservative assumptions.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Workloads:
  - Short QA: user prompt 20–40 tokens, generation 25–45 tokens (primary Helix workload).
  - Long-assist: prompt 200–400 tokens, generation 120–250 tokens (edge cases).
  - Burst profile: 10s microbursts up to 200 qps, steady 40 qps background.

- Test dimensions:
  - Model variants: RDX-3B fp16, RDX-3B int8, RDX-3B int4, RDX-7B fp16 (sanity check).
  - Serving configs: prefix KV cache enabled/disabled, batching windows 0/10/20/40ms, max batch sizes 1/4/8/16, token limit caps (max gen 48 for QA).
  - Hardware: A100x2-per-pod baseline vs H100x1-per-pod comparative run (where applicable).
  - Routing: single-region vs cross-region fallbacks (not heavily exercised for this POC).

Environment details:
- Redwood Dedicated pool (POC staging) in us-east1, 8x A100 80GB across 4 nodes for primary tests.
- Autoscaling off for controlled measurements.
- Network: VPC overlay with ~600us intra-pod median latencies recorded.
- Load driver: workload-generator v2.3 (github link above), open-loop driver to create realistic inter-arrivals (Poisson + burst injection).
- Telemetry: per-request traces, token-level breakdown, kernel time breakdown (where available).

Representative numbers (short QA workload, sustained 40 qps):
- RDX-3B fp16, no cache, no batching: p50 140ms, p95 310ms, p99 430ms, throughput stable at 40 qps.
- RDX-3B fp16, KV cache with 32MB prefix store (cache hit 36%): p50 115ms (hit 70ms / miss 160ms), p95 250ms, p99 380ms.
- RDX-3B int4, KV cache on, batching (max 6, window 15ms): p50 98ms, p95 210ms, p99 340ms, cost -28% vs baseline.
- RDX-7B fp16, KV cache on, batching: p95 360ms (too high for target), cost ~2.3x RDX-3B baseline.

Observations and micro-insights:
- KV cache effectiveness is highly traffic-shape dependent. Helix has ~40% repeat prefixes in the first 6 weeks of sample traffic, but that could vary widely by feature. We recommend collecting production prefix entropy metrics before committing to heavy caching assumptions.
- Small dynamic batching works well if request inter-arrival is smooth. Under spikey microbursts, batching can increase p99 spikes. Consider burst isolation tiers (dedicated small pool for <=1 token responses).
- Quantization (int4) is a strong win here: reduces kernel times, memory pressure, and hence makes it feasible to consolidate more qps per GPU. Ensure Helix runs full-generation-quality evals for their top 150 prompts to validate no clinically relevant hallucination regressions.
- Kernel scheduling: H100 shows less variance in tail than A100 for this workload; if Helix prioritizes tail-latency SLAs they should evaluate H100 pool pricing vs expected SLA penalties.

Cost sensitivity breakdown (per 1k requests, approximate):
- Baseline RDX-3B fp16: $0.72/1k
- +KV cache (36% hit) effective cost: $0.58/1k
- +int4 quant: $0.52/1k
- RDX-7B fp16 baseline: $1.65/1k
- Notes: cost numbers include amortized GPU runtime and Redwood platform overhead, normalized to Helix contract pricing (we used their proposed dedicated commitment discounts).

Quality checks performed:
- Ran 150 domain prompts through each model/config. Measured exact-match on key entities and a simple hallucination score (syntactic contradictions). Int4 had negligible exact-match drop (~<1.2% absolute). For regulatory-sensitive outputs we flagged 12 prompts for deeper review.

Actionable recommendations (short list):
- Phase 1 (next 2 weeks): enable RDX-3B int4 in a canary route for 10% of traffic + KV prefix cache for routable endpoints. Run eval suite nightly.
- Phase 2 (4–8 weeks): enable dynamic batching (max 6, 15ms window) in production for routes with stable arrival shapes. Monitor p99 and rollback window to zero if p99 increases > 20%.
- Phase 3 (8–12 weeks): collect production prefix-hit entropy and evaluate H100 vs A100 dedicated pool for tail improvements.

Runbook snippets (quick ops knobs):
- Lowering p95 quickly when under attack of tail spikes:
  1) roll back batching to window=0 for affected route(s)
  2) enable a low-latency fallback model (RDX-3B-int8) with automatic routing policy (100ms budget)
  3) increase instance concurrency for small-payload-only nodes (dedicated small-pool)

- Cost-optimization checklist:
  - enable prefix KV cache for repeatable templates
  - test int4 quantization with your eval suite before global rollout
  - set conservative batching windows that favor latency for premium routes

Open questions for Helix engineering: (we should get answers before next run)
- How stable is their prompt template distribution month-over-month? If prefixes are highly dynamic, caching benefit disappears quickly.
- Do they prefer SLA guarantees over soft SLOs? This determines whether to invest in H100 for tail guarantees.
- Which endpoints can accept slightly higher p95 in exchange for cost savings? We need a mapping of product endpoints to latency tiers.

Appendix A — detailed raw tables (attached in linked artifacts):
- Full CSVs with per-request traces and token-level time breakdowns (see github results).
- Sample evaluation prompts and human-annotated quality notes.

Notes to internal team:
- Prioritize creating a small ops template to flip KV cache on/off per-route and expose prefix-hit metric in Redwood Console UI for Helix.
- Engineering: schedule a short kernel investigation with runtime team to verify int4 path stability on H100 for our quantized builds.

Next steps (owners):
- Marisol: set up canary route and schedule midnight run of the 150-prompt eval nightly (due 2028-07-28).
- Ethan: add per-route prefix entropy dashboard and link to Helix contract notes (due 2028-08-04).
- Priya: coordinate Helix QA team to review the 12 flagged prompts and sign off on acceptable hallucination risk (due 2028-08-10).

——
Informal notes / scratchpad (raw):
- Observed a weird 20–30ms bump at ~20 qps on node-3 during RDX-3B-int4 runs; possibly NUMA/interconnect jitter. Follow-up with SRE.
- Customer asked about hybrid approach: RDX-3B-int4 for standard users + RDX-7B for premium analysts. Cost delta seems large but feasible. Need pricing model.
- Slack thread: #helix-poc (see channel) has screenshots of console heatmaps and some manual traces.

End of note.
